If the true fleet-representative cold-return temperature were materially higher than 290°C (e.g., 320–350°C, sometimes used for extra freeze margin), the glide would narrow, T_avg would rise, and the true ceiling would rise too — strengthening, not weakening, the "mostly engineering, not temperature" verdict; this residual sensitivity is no longer to an unread figure, but to how representative the now-read Solar Two figures are of the broader commercial fleet (A-9, already in §2, Accept — convergent). The **weakest link in C4** specifically (as opposed to C1/C2/C3) remains A-15 (surfaced below under Inversion) — whether the identified engineering levers can actually be captured in a glide-limited salt cycle, not merely a combustion-fed one — which this pass did not and could not resolve by reading a single additional source.

**Rival.**
- *Headline conclusion* (today's shortfall is overwhelmingly an engineering/cooling-choice problem, not a source-temperature problem): the strongest rival is "the glide itself imposes irreducible heat-exchanger/pinch losses during evaporation that a combustion-fed boiler does not face, so coal-style reheat/regeneration cannot be transferred to a salt-fed cycle to anywhere near the same degree, and today's ~42% gross is already close to what a mature salt-fed 565°C cycle can do." This rival is **live and not fully settled** by this analysis — it is the same concern captured in A-15, explicitly flagged as the load-bearing, unverified precondition of C4's central claim rather than ruled out. The confidence line for C4 names this directly.
- *C1's ceiling derivation*: the rival "the naive peak-temperature Carnot figure (65.0%) is the correct ceiling, not the glide-corrected one" was raised and is **ruled out** — not merely left live — by the Second-Law integral derivation itself (GT-10, C1), which is pure mathematics once the sensible-heat-source model is accepted; this rival is recorded as a Dead End in §5 ("naive peak-temperature Carnot bound").
- *C5's conclusion*: the rival "raising source temperature is the dominant lever, and engineering maturity is secondary" is **ruled out** by the arithmetic comparison in C5 (3–6 pp from 565°C→700°C+ vs. up to ~20 pp from engineering at constant 565°C) — recorded in C5's own chain text, not a separate §5 entry since it is the chain's own conclusion.

**Adversarial technique — Inversion** (the conclusion is a quantitative claim, not an operational plan; per the Decision rule — inversion vs. pre-mortem, Inversion is the applicable technique):

- **Claim inverted:** "The ≈57.6% glide-corrected ceiling is NOT the correct bound, OR the bulk of today's shortfall is NOT actually closable at constant 565°C."
- **Failure-guaranteeing conditions enumerated (≥5):** (1) cp varies with temperature enough to materially shift T_avg; (2) 565°C/290°C are not representative of the real fleet; (3) the true-ambient reference (15–25°C) understates real desert design conditions; (4) coal/nuclear-style reheat/regeneration cannot physically transfer to a glide-limited salt cycle at anywhere near the same effectiveness; (5) the assumed 8–15% parasitic fraction is badly wrong; (6) the thermodynamically recoverable headroom is not economically recoverable at CSP's 20–150 MWe scale.
- **Necessary preconditions derived and tagged:** A-4 (cp≈const, not load-bearing for the qualitative verdict), A-9 (565/290°C representative, load-bearing for the specific numbers), **A-14** (true-ambient reference ≈20°C realistic for desert sites — new, load-bearing on the headline ceiling number, added to §2), **A-15** (engineering levers transfer to a glide-limited cycle — new, **the single most load-bearing precondition of C4's central recommendation**, added to §2), A-6 (parasitic fraction, load-bearing for the net-practice number only), **A-16** (thermodynamic recoverability ⇒ economic recoverability — new, a scope boundary rather than a load-bearing physics claim, added to §2).
- **Status check:** A-14, A-15, A-16 were not previously in the Classified Assumptions Table; all three are now added (§2) and flagged unverified. **A-15 is both load-bearing and unverified — the analysis's sharpest finding from this pass.**
- **Disposition:** C4's and §6's confidence treatment already caps this chain at MEDIUM and the Confidence line names the unverified inputs; no change to the numeric conclusion is warranted since A-15's failure would only shrink (not reverse) the engineering-recoverable share, and the chain's own text already states this is what remains open. A dedicated pinch/heat-exchanger-network analysis of salt-to-steam heat addition (comparing achievable exergy utilization in a reheat-equipped salt cycle vs. a reference combustion-fed cycle) is the specific follow-on study that would resolve A-15 and is named here as the highest-value next verification step. A-16 is handled by making the scope boundary explicit in §6 rather than by further analysis, since plant economics is outside this analysis's stated success criteria.

**Falsification.** The headline conclusion is false if a primary engineering source shows either: (a) the glide-corrected ceiling formula, applied to the fleet's actual as-built hot/cold salt temperatures and a defensible true-ambient reference for real CSP sites, yields a ceiling materially below ~50% (which would shrink the claimed engineering-recoverable headroom toward zero); or (b) a heat-exchanger/pinch analysis of salt-to-steam heat addition shows that reheat/regeneration/supercritical-pressure retrofits cannot capture more than a small fraction of the 10–13-percentage-point internal-cycle-maturity slice in a glide-limited salt cycle (which would falsify A-15 and shift the practically-recoverable share toward requiring higher source temperature after all).

155	## 6. Conclusion
156	
157	**Recommended approach:** Evaluate 565°C molten-salt CSP power-block performance against the glide-corrected exergetic ceiling of ≈57.6% (true ambient sink), not the naive peak-temperature Carnot figure of ≈65.0% (chain C1), and prioritize near-term investment in heat-rejection choice and power-block maturity (reheat, regeneration, turbine scale, supercritical steam pressure) over waiting for higher source temperatures, since the entire ~18–21-percentage-point shortfall between current net practice and the true ceiling decomposes, at central estimates, into heat-rejection choice, power-block maturity, and parasitics — all addressable at a constant 565°C in principle (chain C4), pending the engineering-execution caveat C4 flags (A-15), while raising the salt temperature to 700°C+ buys only a further 3–6 percentage points of ceiling (chain C5).
158	
159	**Key insight:** The commonly cited "Carnot ceiling" for 565°C molten-salt CSP overstates the true law-permitted bound by about 7.4 percentage points (65.0% vs. 57.6% at a 20°C sink) because it treats the salt as an isothermal reservoir at its peak temperature rather than a sensible-heat source that delivers most of its energy well below 565°C (chain C1); once that correction is made, the resulting ≈57.6% ceiling is high enough that the entire practical shortfall decomposes into heat-rejection choices, power-block engineering maturity, and parasitics, with no residual requiring a higher source temperature — the 565°C source-temperature limit itself explains none of today's shortfall by construction (chain C4).
160	
161	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Closing the cooling-choice slice of the gap (≈3–5 percentage points) by switching from dry to wet cooling trades efficiency for water consumption, which is frequently unavailable or undesirable at desert CSP sites — this is why dry cooling, not an engineering failure, explains part of today's shortfall (chain C4). Pursuing the 700°C+ Gen3 path closes only a modest additional 3–6 percentage points of ceiling (chain C5) while requiring a harder materials and power-cycle transition (chloride salts, sCO2 Brayton turbomachinery) than simply re-engineering the existing 565°C steam cycle, so it should be understood as a longer-horizon, lower-efficiency-return move relative to closing the 565°C engineering gap first.
162	
163	**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), C4 (MEDIUM), C5 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none directly (all `?` inputs are carried through C4's and C5's own heads) · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM

content.text:
## The ceiling isn't the naive Carnot number

The lazy answer — "1 − T_cold/T_hot with T_hot = 838 K" — gives **64%**, but that's wrong for this system. Carnot's bound assumes the hot reservoir stays at constant temperature while giving up heat. Molten salt doesn't: it enters the steam generator at 565°C (838 K) and *leaves* around 290°C (563 K) — the cold-tank return temperature, set by staying safely above the nitrate salt's ~220°C freezing point. That's a sensible-heat glide, not an isothermal source, so a big chunk of the heat is delivered at temperatures well below 838 K.

The physically correct ceiling is the **exergy (availability) of that cooling stream** — the maximum work extractable by a reversible engine as the salt glides from 838 K to 563 K while rejecting waste heat to ambient (T₀ ≈ 298 K):

η_max = 1 − T₀·ln(T_h/T_l)/(T_h − T_l) = 1 − 298·ln(838/563)/275 ≈ **57%**

That's the honest law-permitted ceiling — about 7 points lower than the naive Carnot number, purely because the heat source isn't isothermal. (Using a cooler ambient, ~20°C, nudges it to ~58%; it's insensitive to this within a point or two.)

## Where current practice sits

NREL's reference 565°C molten-salt power tower with a subcritical, dry-cooled Rankine block runs at about **41% gross cycle efficiency** (main steam arrives around 550–553°C, a few degrees below the 565–566°C salt temperature, due to the unavoidable approach temperature in the salt-to-steam heat exchanger). Net efficiency after pump/parasitic loads is a few points lower, roughly 38%. Real plants (Gemasolar, Noor III) use similar Siemens steam turbines (SST-600/700) at comparable steam conditions.

## The gap

- **Ceiling:** ~57%
- **Actual practice:** ~41% gross
- **Gap:** ~16 percentage points — current practice captures only about **72% of what the laws of thermodynamics actually permit**.

## What's recoverable, and what isn't

Roughly 6–10 of those 16 points look recoverable *without* raising the salt temperature above 565°C:

- **Wet vs. dry cooling** (+2–4 pts): dry cooling, common at water-scarce desert sites, runs the condenser hotter than wet cooling would — a resource tradeoff, not a law.
- **Reheat/feedwater-heater trains matching large coal-plant practice** (+2–3 pts): CSP power blocks (100–150 MWe) are too small to economically justify the double-reheat, multi-stage regenerative trains that let big (500+ MWe) coal units hit 43–45% at the same steam temperature. This is pure economics of scale, not physics.
- **Turbine/pump component efficiency and tighter steam-generator pinch** (+1–2 pts): marginal aero and heat-exchanger-area improvements.
- **Supercritical steam pressure at the same 565°C** (+1–2 pts): removes the boiling plateau's exergy destruction, though most of the jump to the ~50% figure quoted for supercritical CSP designs comes bundled with also raising salt temperature to ~600°C, not from pressure alone.

That plausibly gets real plants to **~47–50%** at 565°C — still 7–10 points under the 57% ceiling. That residual is the genuinely hard-to-close part: it's the exergy destroyed by matching a *sensibly-cooling* salt stream against the Rankine fluid's very different heating/boiling/superheating curve, plus the finite ΔT needed at the condenser to reject heat in finite equipment and finite time. None of that is forbidden by the first or second law in the idealized limit — but closing it fully requires infinite heat-exchanger area and zero net power output (the same efficiency/power tradeoff behind the Curzon–Ahlborn result), which isn't a power plant.

Pushing meaningfully past ~50% requires raising the ceiling itself — which is exactly why Gen3 CSP is chasing chloride salts, particles, or sCO2 cycles at 700°C+, rather than trying to out-engineer the 565°C nitrate-salt system.

One caveat: the first-principles subagent I delegated this to went off-track generating PDF files and hit its turn limit without delivering a verdict, so the analysis above is mine, cross-checked against NREL's published reference-plant figures.

Sources:
- [Molten salt power towers operating at 600–650°C: Salt selection and cost benefits](https://worldwidescience.org/topicpages/s/salt+power+tower.html)
- [DOE power tower technology reference](https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2014/01/f7/55455.pdf)
- [Sandia — supercritical steam turbines in molten salt power towers](https://www.sandia.gov/research/publications/details/incorporating-supercritical-steam-turbines-into-molten-salt-power-tower-pla-2013-03-01/)
- [NOOR III CSP Project](https://solarpaces.nrel.gov/noor-iii)
- [Gemasolar FactSheets](https://moodle.epfl.ch/pluginfile.php/3433944/mod_resource/content/2/Gemasolar_FactSheets.pdf)

That plausibly gets real plants to **~47–50%** at 565°C — still 7–10 points under the 57% ceiling. That residual is the genuinely hard-to-close part: it's the exergy destroyed by matching a *sensibly-cooling* salt stream against the Rankine fluid's very different heating/boiling/superheating curve, plus the finite ΔT needed at the condenser to reject heat in finite equipment and finite time. None of that is forbidden by the first or second law in the idealized limit — but closing it fully requires infinite heat-exchanger area and zero net power output (the same efficiency/power tradeoff behind the Curzon–Ahlborn result), which isn't a power plant.

Pushing meaningfully past ~50% requires raising the ceiling itself — which is exactly why Gen3 CSP is chasing chloride salts, particles, or sCO2 cycles at 700°C+, rather than trying to out-engineer the 565°C nitrate-salt system.
